blocks.html: Think of a library. A new book has to be brought in and catalogued, it has to sit on a shelf, and later someone has to find it and take it down. Memory works in the same three stages.

head: Stage
What happens
In the library
rows: You take the information in and make sense of it.
The book is brought in and catalogued.
Your brain keeps it over time.
The book sits on the shelf.
You pull it back out when you need it.
Someone finds the book and takes it down.

blocks.html: A memory can fail at any of the three stages. Good memory habits help each one: make it vivid to encode it, space it out so it stays stored, and pull it from your head to make retrieval stronger.
That is the whole system on the infographic Remember It on Purpose: ENCODE, then SPACE, then RETRIEVE. Each technique in this course helps one or more of those stages.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Ana read a page about volcanoes while watching a video. The next day she could not remember a single fact. Which stage most likely failed?
steps: She could not retrieve anything at all, not even with hints.
Her attention was split, so the facts were never encoded well.
A memory that never went in can't be stored or retrieved.
blocks.a: Encoding. The facts were never taken in properly.

blocks.title: Another example
blocks.q: Ben knew the capital of Peru last month but can't recall it now. When a friend says "It starts with L," he says, "Lima!" Which stage was the trouble?
steps: The memory was still stored: a small hint brought it back.
So the trouble was finding it.
blocks.a: Retrieval. The memory was there; he needed a cue to find it.

blocks.html: Thinking memory is one thing you either have or don't. It is a process with three stages, and each one can be trained.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)
Grokipedia: Encoding (memory)
Grokipedia: Memorization

blocks.html: When someone reads you a phone number, you hold it in your head for a few seconds while you dial. That short-term holding place is called working memory. Think of it as a small workbench: you can work on a few things there, but it fills up fast.

In 1956 the psychologist George Miller noticed that people could repeat back about seven items, give or take two. Later work, gathered by Nelson Cowan in 2001, showed that when people can't rehearse or group the items, the true limit is closer to four chunks, usually three to five.
Working memory holds about four chunks. A chunk is any unit you already know as one thing: a digit, a word, a familiar year like 1776.

blocks.name: mm-chunks
blocks.cap: Twelve loose digits overflow the bench. Three familiar years fit easily.

blocks.html: If the bench holds about four things, a twelve-digit number is too much as twelve digits. But if those digits form three years you already know, the bench only has to hold three things.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You hear the list: cat, lamp, river, pencil, cloud, drum, apple, shoe. About how many can most people hold at once without grouping?
steps: Working memory holds about four chunks.
Eight unrelated words is about twice that.
blocks.a: About four, so the list needs grouping or practice.

blocks.html: Thinking a bigger effort will hold more. The workbench is small for everyone. The trick is to make each item on it bigger by chunking, or to move it into long-term memory with practice.

sources.name: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review 63(2)
Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Your workbench is small, but your long-term memory is enormous. It holds the words you know, the faces of your family, how to ride a bike and the story of your last birthday.
Long-term memory is not like a box that fills up. The more you know about a subject, the easier it is to learn more, because each new fact has old facts to connect to.
The real challenge is finding a memory when you need it. A memory with many connections, like a book listed under several subjects in a library catalogue, is easier to find.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Maya knows a lot about horses. Her brother knows little. Both read the same article about a new horse breed. Who will probably remember more a week later, and why?
steps: Maya has many old facts to connect the new ones to.
Connected facts are easier to store and find.
blocks.a: Maya, because new facts link to what she already knows.

blocks.html: This is why building knowledge step by step works: each rung gives the next one something to hold on to.
Cramming new facts with nothing to connect them to. Ask, "What does this remind me of? What do I already know that fits here?"

sources.name: Grokipedia: Encoding (memory)
Grokipedia: Memorization

blocks.html: Try this: what is on the back of a coin you use often? Most people have seen it thousands of times and still can't draw it. They never paid attention to it, so it was never encoded.
Attention is the doorway to memory. To remember something, give it your full attention for a short time.

items: Put away screens while you study.
Study in short, focused blocks instead of long, drifting ones.
Ask yourself a question before you read, so you are looking for the answer.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which study setup gives the best chance to encode a list of spelling words?
steps: A: practicing while a video plays.
B: ten focused minutes at a quiet table, saying and writing each word.
Only B gives the words full attention.
blocks.a: B, ten focused minutes with nothing competing for attention.

blocks.html: Thinking you can do two thinking jobs at once. You switch back and forth, and each switch costs attention.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Encoding (memory)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Here are two ways to learn that the heart has four chambers. One: say "four chambers" ten times. Two: ask why. The heart is two pumps side by side, one to the lungs and one to the body, and each pump has a room that receives blood and a room that pushes it out. Two pumps times two rooms is four.
When you ask why and how, you connect the new fact to things you already know. Those connections are what make a memory easy to find later.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which question helps you remember that the Nile flows north?
steps: "How many times can I say it?" adds no meaning.
"Where is the high ground, and where is the sea?" connects the fact to how rivers work: rivers flow downhill to the sea, and the Nile's sea, the Mediterranean, lies to its north.
blocks.a: Asking where the high ground and the sea are.

blocks.html: Thinking about meaning is a kind of encoding. Memory researchers call it elaboration: adding details and links to a new fact.
Using a memory trick in place of understanding. A trick can hold a fact in place, but understanding gives it roots.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Encoding (memory)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: You know the feeling: a word is on the tip of your tongue. Someone says the first sound and it pops out. The memory was there all along. You needed a cue.
Memories are found through cues. The more cues you build while learning, the more ways back in you have.

items: First letters: HOMES gives you the first letter of each Great Lake.
Places: in a memory palace, each spot in the house is a cue.
Pictures: a sketch you drew is a cue for the facts you labeled.
Questions: a flashcard's front side is a cue for its back.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Leo forgets the third planet from the Sun until he pictures the planets in a row from the Sun outward: Mercury, Venus... Earth! What served as his cue?
steps: Picturing the order gave him a path to follow.
Each planet led to the next.
blocks.a: The order of the planets: each one cued the next.

blocks.html: Every technique in this course builds cues: an acronym is a cue of letters, a palace is a cue of places, chunking makes a few big cues out of many small items.
Building only one cue. If that one fails, you are stuck. A sketch plus a sentence plus a place gives three roads in.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Encoding (memory)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: In the 1880s a German scientist, Hermann Ebbinghaus, tested his own memory with great care. He learned lists of made-up syllables like DAX and BOK, then measured how much he had forgotten after twenty minutes, an hour, a day, a week and a month. He published his results in 1885.
He found a clear shape. Forgetting is fast at first, then it slows down. Much of what he forgot was gone within the first day; after that, what remained faded slowly.

blocks.name: mm-curve
blocks.cap: The forgetting curve: a steep drop at first, then a slow tail. Illustrative shape.

blocks.html: The forgetting curve drops steeply right after learning and then flattens. That means the first day or two matter most.
He also found something hopeful. Each time he relearned a list, it was forgotten more slowly the next time. Reviews at the right time reset the curve and make it flatter.

blocks.name: mm-curve
blocks.cap: With reviews on days 1, 3, 7 and 21, memory comes back up each time and falls more slowly afterward.

blocks.html: Ebbinghaus used nonsense syllables on purpose, so that meaning would not help some items more than others. Meaningful material is forgotten more slowly, but the shape of the curve is similar.
Reading the curve as exact for everyone. It is a shape, not a law with fixed numbers. How fast you forget depends on the material, how well you learned it and how you review.

sources.name: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (English translation, 1913)
Grokipedia: Forgetting curve
Grokipedia: Hermann Ebbinghaus
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: A forgetting-curve graph has two axes. The bottom axis is time, in days after learning. The side axis is how much you remember, from nothing at the bottom to everything at the top.

items: The solid line shows memory with reviews. Each jump up is a review: you recall it again and memory returns to the top.
After each jump the line falls more slowly than the time before.
The dashed line shows memory with no reviews: it drops and stays low.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: On the graph above, about how much is remembered just before the first review, compared with just before the day-21 review?
steps: Find the dip just before day 1: the line is low, near the middle.
Find the dip just before day 21: the line has fallen only a little from the top.
blocks.a: Less before day 1; much more before day 21, because each review slowed the fall.

blocks.html: A steeper drop means faster forgetting. A flatter line means the memory is getting stronger.
Reading the exact numbers off an illustrative curve. These pictures show a shape. Use them to compare, not to predict a score.

sources.name: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (English translation, 1913)
Grokipedia: Forgetting curve
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Ebbinghaus did not only ask what he could recall. He also timed how long it took to relearn a list until he knew it perfectly again. Relearning was always quicker than learning the first time. He called the time saved the savings.
Savings (percent) = (first learning time − relearning time) ÷ first learning time × 100.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A list took 20 minutes to learn. A week later it took 8 minutes to relearn. What were the savings?
steps: Time saved: 20 − 8 = 12 minutes.
blocks.a: 60 percent savings.

blocks.title: Another example
blocks.q: Learning took 30 minutes and relearning took 30 minutes. What does that tell you?
steps: 30 − 30 = 0 minutes saved.
0 percent savings: nothing was kept.
blocks.a: 0 percent: as if learning from scratch.

blocks.html: Savings show that forgetting is rarely complete. A memory you can't pull up may still be partly stored, and a review rebuilds it fast. That is why short reviews work.
Giving up on a subject you "forgot." A quick review costs much less than the first learning.

sources.name: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology (English translation, 1913)
Grokipedia: Hermann Ebbinghaus

blocks.html: Suppose you have one hour to learn your spelling words. You could study for one hour on Thursday night. Or you could study for fifteen minutes on four different days. Same hour, very different results.
Spacing: study sessions spread out over time beat the same amount of study packed into one session, especially for remembering weeks and months later.

This is one of the best-tested findings in the science of learning. A 2006 review by Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues pulled together hundreds of experiments and found spaced practice beat massed practice again and again. It also found that the longer you want to remember, the longer the gaps between reviews should be.

A review works best when the memory has started to fade but is still there. Pulling up a fading memory takes effort, and that effort is what strengthens it. When you cram, the memory never fades between repetitions, so each repetition does less.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Two students each study 60 minutes. Sam: 60 minutes on Sunday. Tess: 15 minutes on Sunday, Monday, Wednesday and Saturday. The test is in three weeks. Who likely remembers more?
steps: Both used 60 minutes.
Tess spread hers over several days.
Spaced practice wins on later tests.
blocks.a: Tess.

blocks.html: Judging a method by how it feels the next morning. Cramming wins tomorrow and loses next month.

sources.name: Cepeda, N. J., and others (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin 132(3)
Grokipedia: Spacing effect
Pashler, H., and others (2007). Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (IES practice guide)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: The infographic gives a simple schedule. On the day you learn something, recall it once right away. Then recall it again on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 21.
Count every day from the day you learned it (day 0). Day 1 is the next day; day 3 is three days after learning; and so on. Each gap is longer than the one before.

blocks.name: mm-calendar
blocks.cap: Learn on the 1st; review on the 2nd, 4th, 8th and 22nd.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You learn a poem on March 5. When are the four reviews?
steps: Day 1: March 5 + 1 = March 6.
Day 3: March 5 + 3 = March 8.
Day 7: March 5 + 7 = March 12.
Day 21: March 5 + 21 = March 26.
blocks.a: March 6, 8, 12 and 26.

blocks.title: Crossing into a new month
blocks.q: You learn a list on April 20. When is the day-21 review? (April has 30 days.)
steps: April 20 + 10 days reaches April 30.
11 more days reaches May 11.
blocks.a: May 11.

blocks.html: At each review: recall first, then check. Reread only what you missed. Missed items come back sooner; easy ones can wait longer.

A starter schedule, not a law. The research supports spacing and growing gaps; it does not prove 1, 3, 7 and 21 are the best numbers for everything. They are easy to remember and work well. If you need it for months, keep going: a review every month or two.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)
Cepeda, N. J., and others (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin 132(3)
Grokipedia: Spacing effect

blocks.html: Life is busy, so it helps to know how to find the next review quickly.
1. Find the learning day (day 0). 2. See which of days 1, 3, 7, 21 are done. 3. Add the next number to the learning date.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Jada learned the Great Lakes on October 10. She reviewed on October 11 and October 13. When is her next review?
steps: Oct 11 is day 1. Oct 13 is day 3.
Next is day 7.
October 10 + 7 = October 17.
blocks.a: October 17.

blocks.title: Crossing a month
blocks.q: Omar learned a list on the 25th of a 31-day month and has done days 1, 3 and 7. When is day 21?
steps: So it is the 15th of the next month.
blocks.a: The 15th of next month.

blocks.html: Counting from the learning day keeps the gaps growing: 1 day, then 2 more, then 4 more, then 14 more.
Skipping a review and starting over. If you miss one, do it as soon as you can and carry on.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Many homeschool families, especially those who follow Charlotte Mason, keep a memory-work box: a shoebox or recipe box with index cards and tabs. It is spaced review on paper, the same idea that flashcard apps use.

blocks.name: mm-box
blocks.cap: Tabs from front to back: Daily, Odd and Even, Monday to Sunday, then 1 to 31.

head: Tab
When the card comes up
Times in a 30-day month
rows: every other day (odd or even dates)

blocks.html: A new card starts on Daily. When it is solid, it moves back: to Odd or Even, then to a weekday, then to a date. Each move means it comes up less often, just like the growing gaps of 1-3-7-21.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A card behind the Even tab. The month has 31 days. How many times will it come up?
steps: That is 30 ÷ 2 = 15 dates.
blocks.a: 15 times.

blocks.title: Another example
blocks.q: A card is behind the Wed tab. The month starts on a Monday and has 30 days. How many times will it come up?
steps: The 1st is Monday, so the 3rd is the first Wednesday.
Wednesdays: 3, 10, 17, 24. Next would be 31, which is past 30.
blocks.a: 4 times.

blocks.html: Moving a card back before it is solid. If you miss it, move it forward to a tab that comes up more often.
For parents. Keep it short: five to ten minutes a day. Say each card aloud first, then check. The Daily tab should stay small, a handful of new things at a time.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)
Grokipedia: Charlotte Mason
Grokipedia: Spacing effect

blocks.html: In 2006, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke gave college students short passages to learn. Some students read a passage four times. Others read it once and then tried three times to write down everything they could remember, without looking.

Five minutes later, the readers did better. But a week later, the group that had practiced recalling remembered far more. The readers had forgotten about half of what they knew; the recallers had kept most of it.
Retrieval practice: trying to recall something, before you look, makes the memory stronger. This is called the testing effect.
Each time you pull a memory out, you strengthen the path to it. Rereading puts the information in front of you, so your memory doesn't have to do the work.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which plan uses the testing effect for learning ten science words?
steps: Plan A: read the list five times.
Plan B: read it once, then cover the meanings and try to say each one, checking after each try.
Only Plan B asks the memory to do the work.
blocks.a: Plan B.

blocks.html: Thinking a test only measures. In these studies, the test itself was the study session that worked best.

sources.name: Roediger, H. L., and Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science 17(3)
Grokipedia: Testing effect
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: When you read a page a second time, it feels easy. The words look familiar, and that smooth feeling tells you, "I know this." But recognizing a page is not the same as being able to produce what is on it with the book closed.

In 2008, Karpicke and Roediger had students learn 40 word pairs in Swahili and English. Once a student got a pair right, some students kept studying it, and some kept being tested on it. A week later, students who kept being tested remembered about 80 percent. Those who stopped being tested, even if they kept studying, remembered only about 35 percent.
The students did not see it coming. Asked to predict their scores, every group guessed about the same, around half.
Your feeling of knowing is a poor guide. The honest check is to close the book and try to recall.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Zoe rereads her notes three times and feels sure. Kai reads once, closes the notes, writes what he remembers, and finds two gaps. Who has the more accurate picture of what they know?
steps: Zoe's sureness comes from familiarity.
Kai tested himself and found real gaps.
blocks.a: Kai, and he also strengthened what he recalled.

blocks.html: Dropping items from practice as soon as you get them right once. In the 2008 study, dropping items from testing was what hurt; keep them in the review.

sources.name: Karpicke, J. D., and Roediger, H. L. (2008). The critical importance of retrieval for learning. Science 319
Roediger, H. L., and Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science 17(3)
Grokipedia: Testing effect
Grokipedia: Desirable difficulty

blocks.html: Narration is the simplest retrieval practice there is. Charlotte Mason, a British educator in the late 1800s, made it the center of her schooling: read a passage once, attentively, then close the book and tell it back.

items: Read or hear one short section.
Close the book. Tell it back aloud, write it, or draw it.
Check against the book. Note only what was missed.
Revisit the misses, then tell it back again.

blocks.html: No peeking while you narrate. The effort of pulling it out is what strengthens it.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: After a chapter about the Pilgrims, a nine-year-old says, "First they sailed on the Mayflower, then they landed and built houses." The parent checks and sees the child left out the first winter. What happens next?
steps: Note the gap: the first winter.
Reread only that part.
Ask the child to tell back that part again.
blocks.a: Reread only the missed part, then narrate it again.

blocks.html: Narration is retrieval practice, which the studies support. Putting it in your own words also adds meaning, which helps encoding.
Narration grows with age: young children tell it aloud; older students write narrations, outline them or draw diagrams.
Rereading the whole chapter after a narration. Reread only the gaps.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Charlotte Mason
Roediger, H. L., and Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science 17(3)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: A blank-page recall, sometimes called a brain dump, is narration in writing. Take a blank sheet, set a timer for a few minutes, and write or sketch everything you remember about a topic.

items: Write everything you can, in any order.
When you are stuck, wait. Ask yourself questions: Who? When? Why?
Then open the book and check.
Add what you missed in a different color. Those are the things to review first next time.

blocks.html: The second color is your study list. It shows exactly where to spend the next review.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Rosa does a blank-page recall of the water cycle. She writes evaporation, condensation and precipitation but leaves out collection. What should her next review focus on?
steps: Her page shows three of the four stages.
The missing stage is collection.
blocks.a: Collection, the part she missed.

blocks.html: Recall is harder than recognition, and that effort is what makes memories last. The page also shows you what you know, so you don't waste time on the rest.
Using the blank page only once. Do it again at the next review and watch the second color shrink.

sources.name: Roediger, H. L., and Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science 17(3)
Karpicke, J. D., and Roediger, H. L. (2008). The critical importance of retrieval for learning. Science 319
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Flashcards are retrieval practice in a stack. But the way you use them matters.

items: Say the answer before you flip. Flipping first turns the card into rereading.
One fact per card. Small cards are easier to recall and to check.
Both directions where it helps: word to meaning, and meaning to word.
Sort as you go: missed cards come back sooner; solid ones move back to longer gaps.
Keep them in. A card you knew once still needs spaced reviews.

blocks.html: A flashcard works only when you answer it from memory first.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Ivy flips each card right away and says, "Oh yes, I knew that." What should she change?
steps: She is recognizing, not recalling.
She should say or write the answer first, then flip to check.
blocks.a: Answer first, then flip.

blocks.html: The site's Vocabulary flashcards and language flashcards sort cards for you with spaced review.
Making cards so big they hold a whole paragraph. Split them up.

sources.name: Karpicke, J. D., and Roediger, H. L. (2008). The critical importance of retrieval for learning. Science 319
Grokipedia: Testing effect
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Read this once and look away: F B I C I A U S A. Nine letters is a lot to hold. Now read it as FBI · CIA · USA. Three chunks. Same letters, much easier.
A chunk is a group you already know as one thing. Working memory holds about four chunks, so chunking makes each slot carry more.

items: Look for a pattern you already know: a year, a name, a rhythm.
Bundle 3 to 4 items into one chunk.
Give the chunk a name.
Recall the chunk names first, then unpack each one.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Chunk the letters T V P C D V D in a way that helps.
steps: Look for groups you already know.
TV, PC and DVD are familiar.
blocks.a: TV · PC · DVD: three chunks instead of seven letters.

blocks.html: Grouping 149217761969 as 14 · 92 · 17 · 76 · 19 · 69. That is six random pairs, more chunks than before, and none means anything. The years work because each one is a single idea you already know.

sources.name: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review 63(2)
Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Phone numbers in the United States are written 555-867-5309 rather than 5558675309 for a reason. Groups of three, three and four are easier to hold.
To chunk a number: split it into groups of 3 or 4, and look for groups that already mean something: years, ages, a house number, a repeated digit.

blocks.title: Worked example
steps: Twelve digits. Look for years.
1800, 1812 and 1914 are all years.
blocks.a: 1800 · 1812 · 1914: three chunks.

blocks.title: Another example
blocks.q: Chunk 365246 into groups that mean something.
steps: 365 is the days in a year.
24 is the hours in a day; 6 is left over.
Or 365 and 246.
blocks.a: 365 · 24 · 6 (days in a year, hours in a day, then 6).

blocks.html: Making chunks of one or two digits. Six pairs is still six things to hold; meaningful groups of three or four are better.

sources.name: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review 63(2)
Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Chunking works on words too. Here is a shopping list: apples, milk, bread, carrots, cheese, rolls, yogurt, bananas, bagels. Nine items. Now sort them:
Sort a list into 3 or 4 groups of things that belong together. Remember the group names first, then the items in each.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Group these: robin, oak, salmon, maple, eagle, trout, pine, sparrow, tuna.
steps: Birds: robin, eagle, sparrow.
Trees: oak, maple, pine.
Fish: salmon, trout, tuna.
blocks.a: Three groups of three: birds, trees and fish.

blocks.html: The group name is a cue. Recalling "fish" helps pull out salmon, trout and tuna together.
Making too many groups. Nine groups of one is no help; aim for three or four.

sources.name: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review 63(2)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: It helps to know how many chunks a thing will take, so you can plan.
Chunks = items ÷ chunk size, rounded up. A leftover makes one more (smaller) chunk.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A 10-digit phone number in groups of 3, 3 and 4. How many chunks?
steps: Three groups.
blocks.a: 3 chunks.

blocks.title: With a leftover
blocks.q: A 14-digit number in chunks of 4. How many chunks?
steps: Round up: 3 full chunks and one of 2 digits.
blocks.a: 4 chunks.

blocks.title: Another
blocks.q: How many chunks of 3 for 20 letters?
steps: Round up to 7.
blocks.a: 7 chunks.

blocks.html: If the count is well over four, chunking alone won't hold it at once. Learn it in parts, or give each chunk a spot in a memory palace.

sources.name: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24(1)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: In 1971 the psychologist Allan Paivio described dual coding: the mind keeps words and images in two connected systems. A word that brings a picture to mind, like apple, can be found by either path. Abstract words, like justice, usually have only the word path, and they are harder to remember.

blocks.name: mm-card
blocks.cap: Picture plus words: two paths back to the same memory.

blocks.html: Sketch it, label it, and explain it. The picture and the words each give you a way back.

items: Draw the structure: boxes, arrows, a simple scene.
One label per part. Skip decoration.
Cover the words and explain the picture; then redraw the picture from the words.
Keep the sketch: it is a second path back to the memory.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which note helps more for the parts of a plant?
steps: A: a list of the parts with definitions.
B: a quick sketch of a plant with roots, stem, leaf and flower labeled, plus one line on what each does.
B gives both a picture and words.
blocks.a: B, the labeled sketch.

blocks.html: Thinking you must draw well. Stick figures and boxes are enough; the point is the link between picture and words.

sources.name: Paivio, A. (1971). Imagery and Verbal Processes. New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston
Pashler, H., and others (2007). Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (IES practice guide)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: The memory tricks in this course all depend on images. Some images stick; some slip away. Ancient teachers of memory noticed the difference long ago, and so have modern memory athletes.
A vivid image is concrete (things you can see), big or strange (exaggerated), moving (action beats still), and linked to the fact.

head: Weak image
Vivid image
rows: A washing machine by the door.
A giant washing machine blocking the front door, sloshing suds onto your shoes (Washington).
A huge apple rolling on the mat, wearing a tiny crown (Adams, for Adam's apple).

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You need to remember to buy eggs. Which image is more vivid?
steps: A: a carton of eggs on the counter.
B: eggs hatching on your pillow, and the chicks marching to the store.
B is strange, moving and concrete.
blocks.a: B.

blocks.html: Making an image so silly it has nothing to do with the fact. Test the fact, not the joke: if the image comes back and the fact doesn't, change the image.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Method of loci
Grokipedia: Mnemonic

blocks.html: You may have heard that some people are "visual learners" and others "auditory" or "hands-on" learners, and that each learns best when taught in their own style. It is a popular idea.

In 2008 Harold Pashler and colleagues reviewed the research. To support the idea, a study would need to show that visual learners learn more from a visual lesson and auditory learners learn more from an auditory one. They found almost no studies that showed this, and several that found the opposite.
People do have preferences. But matching lessons to a preferred "style" has not been shown to help. What helps is matching the method to the material, and combining pictures and words for everyone.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: A teacher wants her class to learn the parts of the eye. Which plan fits the evidence?
steps: A: draw a labeled eye for the "visual learners" and read the parts aloud for the "auditory learners."
B: everyone sketches and labels the eye, explains each part aloud, then redraws it from memory.
B combines pictures, words and retrieval for all.
blocks.a: B.

blocks.html: A map is best learned by looking, a song by listening, and a dance by moving, for everyone. The material decides.
Thinking this means pictures don't matter. Dual coding helps every learner, which is the point of the infographic's "picture + words."

sources.name: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., and Bjork, R. (2008). Learning styles: Concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest 9(3)
Grokipedia: Learning styles
Paivio, A. (1971). Imagery and Verbal Processes. New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston

blocks.html: An acronym is a word made of first letters. The five Great Lakes are Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior: HOMES. The colors of the rainbow in order are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet: ROY G. BIV.
Use an acronym when the first letters are enough to bring back each item. If order matters, keep the letters in order. If it doesn't, rearrange them into a real word.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Make an acronym for the five senses in any order: sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell.
steps: First letters: S, H, T, T, S.
Order doesn't matter, so look for a word or name.
No neat word comes out, so a phrase may work better: "STTSH" is hard to say.
blocks.a: When no word appears, try an acrostic sentence instead (next topic).

blocks.title: When order matters
blocks.q: Make an acronym for these in order: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
steps: First letters: K P C O F G S.
No word, and order matters.
An acrostic sentence is better here: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.
blocks.a: KPCOFGS, best held with a sentence.

blocks.html: Learning the acronym but not the items. HOMES helps only if you know H is for Huron.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Mnemonic
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: When the first letters don't make a word, make a sentence instead. Each word of the sentence starts with the letter of an item, in order.

head: Sentence
Stands for
rows: My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (the planets from the Sun)
E, G, B, D, F: the notes on the lines of the treble staff, bottom to top
North, East, South, West, clockwise around the compass
King Philip Came Over For Good Soup
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species

blocks.html: A good acrostic is short, easy to picture, and keeps the items in order.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Make an acrostic for the first five U.S. presidents: Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Madison, Monroe.
steps: Letters: W, A, J, M, M.
Find a sentence: "Will A Jolly Man Make..." "Will A Jolly Man Mow?"
blocks.a: Will A Jolly Man Mow? (W, A, J, M, M)

blocks.html: The sentence is a chain of cues. Each word reminds you of the next, and each first letter reminds you of an item.
Picking words that start with the right letter but a different sound, which can mislead you later. Keep the words simple.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Mnemonic
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Long before writing, people kept stories and laws in verse. Rhythm and rhyme give words a shape: if a word is missing, the line sounds wrong, and that tells you to look for it.

items: "In fourteen hundred ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue."
"Thirty days hath September, April, June, and November. All the rest have thirty-one, except February alone..."
The alphabet song, which most English speakers still hum to put words in order.
Skip-counting songs for times tables, and chants of Latin endings (-ō, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt).

blocks.html: Use a song or chant when the sound must stick and the items come in a fixed order.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: "Thirty days hath September, April, June, and November." How many days are in June?
steps: June is named in the rhyme's list of thirty-day months.
blocks.a: 30 days.

blocks.html: A tune holds many words in order with little effort, which is why songs and chants are the most common kind of memory work for young children.
Stopping at the song. The song gets the words in; the next step is to use them: answer the question "What is 7 × 8?" without singing from the start.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Mnemonic
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Learning words in another language? The keyword method builds a bridge in two steps.

items: Sound link: find an English word that sounds like the new word.
Picture link: make a vivid picture joining that English word with the meaning.

head: New word
Means
Sounds like
Picture
rows: A cat swinging on a garden gate.
A duck sitting in a cooking pot, quacking.
A table piled with a messy heap of dishes.
A library where every book has legs.

blocks.html: Sound link plus picture link. Say the word, see the picture, get the meaning.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Spanish perro means dog. Build a keyword picture.
steps: Sound: perro sounds a little like "pear."
Picture: a dog chewing a giant pear.
blocks.a: A dog chewing a giant pear (perro, dog).

blocks.html: Forgetting the true pronunciation. The keyword is a bridge to the meaning; still learn to say the word correctly.

blocks.html: The memory palace, also called the method of loci (Latin for "places"), is one of the oldest memory tools. Roman writers told of the Greek poet Simonides, who after an accident at a banquet could name every guest by remembering where each had sat. Cicero and Quintilian later taught the method to speakers.
You already know the order of the rooms in your home. A memory palace borrows that order: put one vivid image at each spot, and the route hands them back to you in order.

blocks.name: mm-palace

items: washing machine
Adam's apple
a jeffer-SUN
a mad son

blocks.cap: The first presidents along a route: Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Madison.

items: Pick a route you know by heart: front door, mat, mirror, stairs...
Use the same spots, in the same order, each time.
Put one vivid, silly image at each spot. Moving beats still.
Walk the route in your head. Rebuild only the blank spots.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: You place a giant washing machine at the front door to stand for Washington. Why use the front door?
steps: It is spot 1 on your route.
So Washington comes first.
blocks.a: Because spot 1 holds item 1: the route keeps the order.

blocks.html: The house on the infographic is itself a memory palace: walk rooms 1 to 6 and you have recalled all six techniques.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Method of loci
Dresler, M., and others (2017). Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory. Neuron 93(5)
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: The route is the backbone of the palace. A good one is easy to walk in your head and has spots you can tell apart.
A good route: a place you know well, a fixed direction (always clockwise, say), and distinct spots that look different from each other.

head: Good spot
Weak spot
Why
rows: A blank wall has nothing to hang an image on.
the third of six identical chairs
You must see it clearly in your head.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which route is better for ten items?
steps: A: ten spots along your walk from the front door to your bedroom: door, mat, coat hook, mirror, stairs, landing, bathroom sink, bathtub, bedroom door, bed.
B: ten floor tiles in the kitchen.
A's spots are different and in a natural order.
blocks.a: Route A.

blocks.html: Images stick to spots that are easy to picture. If the spots blur, the images blur too.
Building a new palace for every list. The infographic's advice: reuse a few routes you know well.

sources.name: Grokipedia: Method of loci
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Once your images are placed, recalling is a walk. Start at spot 1 and move along the route. At each spot, look for the image and turn it back into the item.

blocks.name: mm-palace

items: milk
eggs
bread
apples
cheese
rice

blocks.cap: A shopping list on a six-spot route. What is at spot 4?

blocks.html: Because every spot has a number, the palace answers questions like "What was fourth?" and "What came after bread?" You can even walk it backward.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Your route: front door, mat, coat hook, mirror, stairs, sofa. You placed: milk, eggs, bread, apples, cheese, rice. What was the fourth item?
steps: Walk: 1 front door (milk), 2 mat (eggs), 3 coat hook (bread), 4 mirror.
The mirror holds apples.
blocks.a: Apples.

blocks.html: The route turns a hard question (what was fourth?) into an easy one (what is at the mirror?).
Skipping the walk at review time. Walk the full route each time; rebuild only the spots that come up blank.

blocks.html: Sleep is not time off for memory. While you sleep, the brain replays and strengthens what it practiced during the day. A large 2010 review by Susan Diekelmann and Jan Born gathered the evidence that sleep supports the consolidation of memories, the process that makes a new memory more stable.
Get enough sleep while you are learning. A short review before bed and a quick check in the morning fit well with how sleep helps.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which plan is better the night before a recitation?
steps: A: stay up past midnight practicing.
B: one practice run after supper, a full night's sleep, and one run at breakfast.
B keeps sleep and adds a morning check.
blocks.a: B.

blocks.html: A memory is fragile at first. Sleep is one of the times it becomes sturdier, so trading sleep for more study often loses more than it gains.
Thinking you can learn something new while you sleep, by playing a recording. Sleep helps keep what you practiced while awake; it is not a way to learn new material.

sources.name: Diekelmann, S., and Born, J. (2010). The memory function of sleep. Nature Reviews Neuroscience 11
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Practice can be blocked: all of one kind, then all of the next (AAA BBB CCC). Or it can be interleaved: kinds mixed together (A C B B A C B A C).

In 2007, Doug Rohrer and Kelli Taylor had college students practice finding the volumes of four kinds of shapes. Blocked students did better during practice, about 89 percent right against 60 percent. But on a test a week later, the mixed students scored 63 percent and the blocked students only 20 percent.
Interleaving: mix problem types or subjects in review. You learn not only how to do each kind, but which kind a problem is.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which review set is interleaved?
steps: A: 5 addition, then 5 subtraction, then 5 multiplication.
B: 15 problems with the three kinds shuffled together.
B mixes the kinds.
blocks.a: B.

blocks.html: With blocked practice you know the method before you read the problem. Mixed practice makes you choose, and choosing is the skill a test asks for.
Mixing on day one of a new skill. Learn the new kind first, then mix it into review.

sources.name: Rohrer, D., and Taylor, K. (2007). The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science 35
Grokipedia: Desirable difficulty
Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: When an older child teaches a younger brother or sister, the older one learns too. To explain something, you have to pull it from memory, put it in order, and answer questions you didn't expect.
Teaching works best from memory: explain it with the book closed, then check what you left out.

items: Explain it in your own words, with no notes.
Use a picture or an example.
Let the learner ask questions; a question you can't answer shows a gap.
Open the book together and check.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Eli explains the water cycle to his sister and gets stuck on why clouds form. What has he found?
steps: Teaching showed a gap in his understanding.
That gap is where to study next.
blocks.a: A gap to review: how water vapor condenses into clouds.

blocks.html: Teaching combines retrieval (pulling it out), meaning (explaining why), and a check (questions). That is three good habits in one.
Reading the lesson aloud to someone and calling it teaching. Without recall, it is rereading.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)
Grokipedia: Testing effect

blocks.html: Every child is different, so treat this as a guide, not a rule. The infographic puts it this way:

head: Ages
Tools that fit
rows: Songs, chants and hand motions; short daily recitation; narration of a short story; picture cards.
Chunking and acronyms; a memory-work box with tabs; narration in writing; a memory palace at home.
Self-testing and blank-page recall; memory palaces with silly images; sketch-and-label notes; their own spaced-review schedule.

blocks.html: Narration and spaced review work at every age; only the form changes.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which tool fits a six-year-old learning the days of the week?
steps: Six is in the 4 to 7 band.
A song or chant fits that age.
blocks.a: A days-of-the-week song with hand motions.

blocks.html: Young children remember sound and rhythm well and don't yet plan their own study. Older students can manage their own schedule, so self-testing and palaces fit.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Here is the infographic's first session, in four steps.

head: Step
What to do
rows: One poem, one list, one set of terms, not the whole chapter.
Pick one tool: a palace, chunks, a sketch or a song.
Close the books and tell it back. Check. Fix only the misses.
Mark day 1, 3, 7 and 21 on the calendar, or file the card in the box.

blocks.html: The recipe: one vivid encode + spaced retrieval. Always finish with a closed-book recall, and put the next review on the calendar before you close the books.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Nora wants to learn the eight parts of speech. Plan her first session.
steps: Choose: the eight parts of speech.
Encode: an acrostic or a memory palace.
Retrieve: close the book, list all eight, check.
Space: mark days 1, 3, 7 and 21.
blocks.a: Choose, encode, retrieve, space.

blocks.html: Ending the session with a reread. End with a recall.

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: Two plans can take the same time and give very different results. Check each plan against four questions.

head: Question
Stronger
Weaker
rows: All of one kind at a time

blocks.html: More hours don't make a better plan. Better habits do.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Plan A: highlight the chapter for two hours the night before. Plan B: four 20-minute sessions over a week, each starting with a blank-page recall. Which is weaker, and why?
steps: A is crammed and uses highlighting, not recall.
B is spaced and uses retrieval.
blocks.a: Plan A is weaker: crammed, no recall.

blocks.html: Counting only time. Plan B above uses less time and works better.

blocks.html: Each technique fits some material better than others.

head: The material
A good fit
Why
rows: Groups of 3 or 4 fit the workbench.
Parts of a structure (a cell, a map)
A sketch shows how the parts fit.
A short list where first letters are enough
Exact words: a poem, a chant, endings
The tune holds the words in order.
Telling it back keeps its meaning and order.

blocks.html: Pick one encode tool that fits the material, then always add spaced retrieval.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Which tool fits the order of the 13 original colonies, north to south?
steps: Thirteen items, and order matters.
A memory palace keeps a long order.
blocks.a: A memory palace (or an acrostic, for the first letters).

sources.name: Teddy Rook Book, Remember It on Purpose (infographic)

blocks.html: You now know the whole system. A good plan answers five questions.

items: What? One small chunk of material.
Which tool? The encode tool that fits the material and the learner's age.
How will I recall? Closed book: narration, blank page or flashcards.
When are the reviews? Days 1, 3, 7, 21 on the calendar, or a card in the box.
What else helps? Sleep, mixing old material into reviews, and teaching someone.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.q: Plan: a 13-year-old wants to learn the first ten elements of the periodic table, starting Monday the 2nd.
steps: What: the first ten elements in order.
Tool: a memory palace with ten spots (age 12+, order matters).
Recall: walk the palace and write the list, then check.
Reviews: day 1 (Tue 3rd), day 3 (Thu 5th), day 7 (Mon 9th), day 21 (Mon 23rd).
Extras: mix the elements into review with other lists; teach a sibling.
blocks.a: A ten-spot palace, closed-book recall, reviews on the 3rd, 5th, 9th and 23rd.

blocks.html: Memory isn't a talent you have. It's a habit you build.
